title: Piezoelectric free-standing thick-film structures for material characterization and energy harvesting applications
venue: 2015 Joint IEEE International Symposium on the Applications of Ferroelectric (ISAF), International Symposium on Integrated Functionalities (ISIF), and Piezoelectric Force Microscopy Workshop (PFM)

sections.heading: Piezoelectric Free-Standing Thick-Film Structures for Material Characterization and Energy Harvesting Applications
sections.text:
Yang Bai, Hana Hughes and Tim W. Button Central European Institute of Technology - CEITEC Brno 616 00, Czech Republic yang.bai@ceitec.vutbr.cz

Yang Bai, Carl Meggs, Yun Jiang, Canlin Ou and Tim W. Button

School of Metallurgy and Materials University of Birmingham - UoB Birmingham B15 2TT, United Kingdom t.w.button@bham.ac.uk

Abstract—This paper reports the fabrication and characterization of a free-standing piezoelectric thick-film structure: single-layer films and multi-layer cantilevers, for the application of vibrational energy harvesting. Piezoelectric properties without constraint effect are properly characterized. The single-layer thick-films exhibit ${ \bf d } _ { 3 1 }$ values of approximately $\mathbf { 1 0 0 \ p C / N }$ , which is much larger than in other reports. This can provide a more reasonable and accurate way to measure real properties of piezoelectric thick-films, and thus offer more reliable data to modelling and design of thick-film structured piezoelectric devices. Flat, free-standing thick-film cantilevers free from residual stress are also fabricated. The requirements of ink composition and sintering procedure are defined. When tested under harmonic vibration conditions, the cantilevers show increases of $2 0 \mathbf { - } 1 2 0 \ \%$ in output power density under different vibration accelerations at their resonant frequencies compared to the reported energy harvesters based on similar materials and structures. This work demonstrates the potential for fabricating co-sintered piezoelectric multi-layer thick-film structures with higher potential flexibility and energy conversion efficiency.

Keywords—piezoelectric, thick-film, free-standing, energy harvesting

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Piezoelectric single-layer (e.g. unimorph) and multi-layer (e.g. bimorph, stack) thick-film structures have been widely used in sensors, actuators, transducers and energy harvesters because of their reduced thickness $( 1 { - } 1 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m } )$ compared to bulk ceramics and better performance compared to thin-films, especially in micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) [1, 2]. In common with other functional ceramic films, piezoelectric thick-films are normally deposited on substrates such as silicon, stainless steel or alumina together with metallic electrodes and then co-sintered. This is to facilitate the fabrication of the devices and integration with electronic circuitry. However, as the piezoelectric phenomenon entails material deformation (or strain) to achieve electromechanical coupling, the existence of an inactive substrate absorbs or dissipates some of the input energy, thus restricting the energy conversion efficiency and electrical output of, for example, piezoelectric vibration energy harvesters. Due to mismatch of the shrinkage of the piezoelectric and electrode layers during the sintering process, and the constraining effect of the already dense substrate, residual stress would also be expected at the layer interfaces, potentially leading to poor ceramic sintering, delamination and breakdown during poling under high electric fields. In addition, the characterization of piezoelectric thick-films on inactive substrates is problematic as the properties of the films cannot be independently measured due to the constraint effect caused by the substrates.

In order to solve the above issues, Kok et al. [2] firstly reported a structure of a piezoelectric free-standing thick-film cantilever. The structures have been successfully fabricated and used for vibrational energy harvesting. However, even though such a reported structure was independent of the inactive substrate, delamination or constraint phenomena were still observed due to mismatch of the shrinkage of the piezoelectric and electrode layers during sintering. As the properties of the piezoelectric composition were not optimized, the energy harvesting output power density was not ideal and, due to the use of Ag-Pd electrodes in the structure, the cost of such devices could be prohibitive. This paper demonstrates an optimized and cost-effective method to fabricate and process piezoelectric free-standing single-layer and piezoelectric/silver co-sintered multi-layer thick-film structures, in order to improve the properties and explore the capabilities of free-standing thick-film structured energy harvesters.

sections.heading: II. EXPERIMENTAL
sections.text:
A commercial ‘soft’ piezoelectric composition – PZT-5H (TRS610C, TRS Technologies, USA), as well as a laboratory-made La-doped PZnN-PZT were used as the piezoelectric elements. Details of these compositions are listed in Table I. The PZT is a commonly used composition for many piezoelectric devices, and it was used as a reference composition in this paper. The doping of La and $\mathrm { P Z n N }$ into the PZT matrix may provide larger piezoelectric voltage coefficient $( g _ { 3 3 }$ and $g _ { 3 I , }$ ) values [3], which is beneficial for energy harvesting. The PZnN-PLZT was synthesized via the conventional solid-state reaction $9 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ calcination) from raw powders of $\mathrm { P b O }$ $( > 9 8 ~ \%$ , BDH Chemical Ltd., USA), $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O } } }$ $( > 9 9 . 5 ~ \%$ , BDH Chemicals Ltd, USA), ${ \mathrm { N b } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 5 }$ $( > ~ 9 9 . 9 ~ \%$ , Fluka Chemika, UK), $\mathrm { L a } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 3 }$ $( > 9 9 ~ \%$ , BDH Chemicals, USA), $Z \mathrm { r } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ $( > 9 9 . 8 2 \ \%$ , Minchem HMP Ltd., UK) and $\mathrm { T i O } _ { 2 }$ $( > 9 9 . 9 \%$ , PI-KEM Ltd., UK), where $1 \ \mathrm { w t } \%$ excess PbO was added in order to compensate for $\mathrm { P b }$ loss during fabrication. The PZT and synthesized PZnN-P3LZT powder were subsequently mixed with a commercial borosilicate glass (acting as low-temperature sintering aid, Particle Technology, UK) and a thick-film vehicle – the Blythe (Johnson Matthey, UK) using a 3-roll mill (G2996/84/484/2, Marchant Engineers, UK), and thus printable ceramic inks were formed. The content of the sintering aid was $1 \ \mathrm { w t } \%$ of the piezoelectric powder, while the ratio of the powder mixture (containing piezoelectric powder and sintering aid) and the vehicle was $80 \mathrm { w t \% }$ and $20 \mathrm { w t \% }$ , respectively. In addition, a silver ink (for the electrodes) comprising $70 \mathrm { w t \% }$ silver flake (FS2, Johnson Matthey, UK) and $3 0 ~ \mathrm { \ w t \% }$ vehicle, and a carbon ink (for the sacrificial layer) comprising $3 0 \ \mathrm { w t \% }$ carbon powder (Monarch 120, Johnson Matthey, UK) and $70 \mathrm { \ m t \% }$ vehicle, were also fabricated in advance. Free-standing single-layer thick-films or unimorph cantilevers were fabricated by a doctor blading process. Schematic diagrams of the fabrication processes are shown in Fig. 1. A $7 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ thick tape (810 Magic, Scotch, UK) and a $1 4 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ thick tape (494-354, RS Components Ltd., UK) were employed to control the thickness of each bladed layer. A carbon layer was deposited onto alumina substrates $ { \mathrm { ~ \textrm ~ { ~ ~ } ~ } } { \mathrm { { I } \ m m } }$ thick, CeramTech North America, USA) first of all, followed by the other layers as shown in Fig. 1. Each layer was dried at $7 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ before printing the next layer. All layers were co-sintered at $8 7 5 { \cdot } 9 5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 0.5-2 hours, during which time the carbon layer was burnt off thus enabling free-standing thick-film structures to be obtained. In further detail, as shown Fig. 1 (a) two series of single-layer films were fabricated, where Series 1 samples were used for measurements of physical properties (e.g. shrinkage) and thus no electrode was coated. In Series 1, not only piezoelectric but also silver single-layer films were fabricated. Series 2 samples were used for measurements of the functional properties of the free-standing piezoelectric layers (e.g. piezoelectric coefficient $d _ { 3 I }$ , relative permittivity $\varepsilon _ { r } ,$ electromechanical coupling coefficient $k _ { 3 I , }$ ), for which Cr-Au electrodes were deposited on both surfaces via sputtering (K575X, Emitech, UK). The planar dimensions of wet films of Series 1 and 2 were $1 0 \times 1 0 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ and $3 \times 1 5 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ , respectively. In Fig. 1 (b), it can be seen that the top electrode was slightly smaller than other layers, in order to avoid shorting during high-voltage poling. sections.heading: A. Ink Properties and the Effect on Free-standing Cantilevers
sections.text:
As the fabrication process of the free-standing structures involved co-sintering silver/piezoelectric multi-layers, the first issue should be to gain a good knowledge of the shrinkage of individual films when subjected to various firing procedures, and their influence on the appearance and integrity of the sintered cantilevers. The planar shrinkage of individual layers of the silver, PZT and PZnN-P3LZT inks at different sintering temperatures with different dwell durations (measured from the Series 1 samples) are shown in Fig. 3. The silver ink had approximately the same shrinkage for all the conditions tested. The main contribution to the shrinkage of the silver ink is considered as polymer decomposition when heated to the sintering temperature. Also, as the tested temperatures shown in Fig. 3 were rather close to the melting point of silver (about $9 6 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ , sintering of the silver ink is expected as well. However, sintering did not affect the planar shrinkage of the silver ink, implying that the silver had achieved the fullest densification under these conditions. In contrast, although polymer decomposition did not contribute to the differences of shrinkage under different conditions for the PZT and PZnN-P3LZT inks, the shrinkage varied for the different sintering procedures as shown in Fig. 3 because of change of densification level. Both sintering temperature and dwell duration had significant influence on the shrinkage. The pictures of some sintered cantilevers corresponding to the P1 to P7 procedures labelled in Fig. 3 are shown in Fig. 4. It can be seen that if the shrinkage of the silver layer was much larger than that of the piezoelectric elements (P1), a delamination problem was likely to occur (Fig. 4 (a)). On the contrary, if the shrinkage of the silver layers were equal to or smaller than that of the piezoelectric layers (P2), the cantilever would deflect downwards and even stick onto the substrate during sintering, leading to a failure to obtain a free-standing structure (Fig. 4 (b)). It was found empirically that only by maintaining a difference of $3 \%$ to $6 \%$ higher value in the overall shrinkage of the silver element compared to that of the piezoelectric elements could a flat, free-standing thick-film cantilever free from residual stress be obtained (Fig. 4 (c) and (d)). The phenomena observed for P3, P6 and P7 were similar to those for P2, P4 and P5, respectively.

sections.heading: B. Properties of Single-layer Thick-films
sections.text:
The dielectric and piezoelectric properties of the two types of thick-films are summarized in Table II, with a comparison to the literature [2] in which free-standing ‘soft’ PZT thick-films were fabricated with sintering temperatures of $8 5 0 – 9 5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . The $g _ { 3 I }$ values were calculated from the $d _ { 3 I }$ divided by $\varepsilon _ { r }$ . As shown in Table II, the PZnN-P3LZT thick-films had larger $d _ { 3 I }$ and $g _ { 3 I }$ values. This would imply a higher theoretical output voltage and off-resonant output power for the harvesters made from such thick-films compared to those made from the PZT thick-films with the same dimensions and peak deflections [2, 5]. However, the resonant output power density and energy conversion efficiency were difficult to evaluate theoretically due to the complex dependencies on the other parameters, e.g. $k _ { 3 I }$ , $Q _ { M } ,$ $\varepsilon _ { r }$ and tan-. In addition, the free-standing PZT thick-film fabricated in this work exhibited smaller $\varepsilon _ { r }$ and $Q _ { M }$ but larger $d _ { 3 I } , \ g _ { 3 I }$ and $k _ { 3 I }$ values compared to those in [2]. sections.heading: C. Vibration Tests of Cantilevers
sections.text:
The output power densities of the PZT and PZnN-P3LZT free-standing cantilevers measured with a range of accelerations at their individual resonant frequencies are shown in Fig. 6. The outputs reached the peaks with a resistive load of $2 2 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ for both types of harvesters with all of the four input accelerations. The optimum average output power densities for the PZnN-P3LZT harvesters were calculated to be $900 \%$ $\left( 0 . 1 \ \mathrm { g } \right)$ , $68 \%$ $( 0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { g } )$ , $73 \%$ $( 1 . 0 \ \mathrm { g } )$ and $173 \%$ $( 1 . 5 \ { \mathrm { g } } )$ better than those of the respective PZT harvesters. When compared to the data obtained on a screen-printed PZT-5H free-standing thick-film unimorph energy harvesters tested at its resonant frequency with $6 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ resistive load [2], the advantages were even more remarkable, approaching to $2 5 \ \%$ $( 0 . 1 \ \mathrm { g } )$ , $92 \%$ $( 0 . 5 \ \mathrm { g } )$ and $1 2 1 \% ( 1 . 0 \ : \mathrm { g } )$ .

sections.heading: IV. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text: Single-layer free-standing piezoelectric thick-films with PZT and PZnN-P3LZT compositions have been fabricated, based on which the planar shrinkage behaviour and the functional properties without constraint effect have been measured. The shrinkage behavior has provided a guidance for the successful co-sintering of silver/piezoelectric multi-layer free-standing cantilevers. The use of silver electrodes should significantly reduce the fabrication cost compared to that of Ag-Pd or Pt electrodes. The improved PZnN-P3LZT functional properties related to energy harvesting have induced an improvement of $20 \mathrm { - } 1 2 0 \ \%$ in output power density under different vibration accelerations compared to the PZT cantilevers produced in this work or reported elsewhere.
